title: Greenpoint, Between Trees and Noise
gallery_text: In my experience, noise in Greenpoint is most noticeable around subway stations and restaurants. The map makes me wonder how transit, nightlife, and street activity shape reported noise, while reminding me that 311 complaints represent residents’ reports rather than sound itself.
description:
This map combines two datasets for ZIP Code 11222, which I use as a practical proxy for Greenpoint, Brooklyn.

The first dataset is the NYC Parks 2015 Street Tree Census (NYC Open Data: uvpi-gqnh). NYC Parks organized the census with volunteers to record the location, species, health, and trunk diameter of individual street trees for urban-forest management and planning. Source: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/uvpi-gqnh

The second dataset is NYC 311 Service Requests from the 2010–2019 archive (NYC Open Data: 76ig-c548). The 311 system collected these records to document service requests and complaints that could be directed to municipal agencies. I selected noise-related requests submitted within ZIP Code 11222 during 2015. Source: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/76ig-c548

Rather than using the datasets for tree management or municipal service tracking, I overlay them to compare Greenpoint’s city-managed street-tree landscape with the uneven geography of reported noise. Noise requests are aggregated into hexagons, while individual street trees remain visible as points. The map does not treat 311 complaints as direct measurements of sound: reporting patterns also reflect residents’ awareness of 311, willingness to report, and expectations about neighborhood noise. Likewise, ZIP Code 11222 is a convenient data boundary but does not perfectly represent residents’ definitions of Greenpoint.
